strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and interesting gap: existing ML-based primal heuristics for MILP focus on binary variables and produce partial solutions delegated to a traditional solver, while this work targets complete feasible solutions with non-binary integer variables.

The RL formulation is clearly described: a well-motivated two-phase reward design (feasibility discovery vs. objective improvement) with an explicit interval-based reward tied to the LP-relaxation lower bound, and a phase token to condition the policy.

The architecture rationale is sensible, combining local message passing on the bipartite MILP graph with a Transformer encoder to capture long-range variable interactions, and this is supported by ablations (Table 3) showing each component (PE, PT, SL) contributes.
An ablation study with qualitative behavioral analysis (e.g., Critic instability without PE, phase bias without PT/SL) provides insight into why components matter, not just that they do.
Limitations are honestly acknowledged in the conclusion (integer-only variables, local-search restriction preventing global optimality).
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is far too narrow to support the central claim of an 'end-to-end ML MILP solver'. Evaluation uses only randomly generated instances from a single generator (Table 1), with sizes of 9x18 and 100x50 variables/constraints. These are trivially easy: Gurobi solves them in under 1 second. No standard benchmarks (MIPLIB, MIRPLib, set covering, etc.) or real-world instances are used.

The headline framing ('eliminate reliance on traditional solvers', Figure 1(b)) is undermined by the method itself: inference requires the LP-relaxation solution and lower bound objr from a traditional solver (Algorithm 1, Line 1), and phase2 rewards are defined in terms of objr. The method is thus a solver-guided local search, not a standalone ML solver.

The baseline comparison is weak and arguably unfair/uninformative: Gurobi is compared under 100-second limits on instances it solves in <1s, and the only other baselines are the authors' own architecture ablations (M_MLP, M_CNN). No comparison against relevant prior ML/RL approaches, e.g., Smart Feasibility Pump (Qi et al. 2021), neural diving (Nair et al. 2020), or predict-and-search (Han et al. 2023), despite these being cited and discussed.

RP Gap is computed against the best objective across compared methods (Eq. 11) rather than a true optimum or a valid lower bound, so '0% RP Gap = optimal' on D9*18 is not actually established, and results on D100*50 lack a certificate of quality.

No statistical rigor: results are single-run averages over 100 instances with no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds; training uses only 500 parameter updates on the small dataset, and no hyperparameter details (layer counts, learning rates, embedding sizes) or code release are provided, harming reproducibility.

The action space (unit +/-1 increments per variable, three actions) is extremely restrictive and clearly does not scale to variables with large or unbounded ranges, which the paper itself motivates as the core challenge; the interaction between step size, delta local region, and reward shaping is not analyzed.

The 'first to incrementally find better complete feasible solutions' novelty claim is overstated: RL-guided local search and improvement heuristics for CO are well established, and the delta between this work and prior feasibility-pump-style RL (Qi et al. 2021) plus a local search wrapper is incremental.

Generalization is untested: training and testing use the same instance distribution; there is no evidence of transfer to other distributions, sizes, or structures, which is the central question for learned solvers.
Sections 2.1-2.3 spend considerable space on textbook preliminaries, while space that could have gone to scaling experiments, baseline comparisons, or variance analysis is missing.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and well-organized; the two-phase reward design (feasibility first, then objective improvement) and the use of a phase token to condition the agent are sensible and easy to follow.

An ablation study (Table 3) is provided for the three architectural components (Periodic Embedding, Phase Token, Separated Layers), and the qualitative explanations of failure modes without each component add some insight.

The problem motivation — handling non-binary integer variables and guaranteeing feasibility — addresses a genuine gap in ML-based primal heuristics, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges the local-search restrictions and integer-only scope.
weaknesses: The central claim of solving MILP 'without delegating the remainder to traditional solvers' / 'based solely on ML' is not supported by the method itself: the algorithm requires an LP-relaxation solved by a traditional solver to obtain both the initial solution x0 and the lower bound obj_r used in the phase-2 reward (Algorithm 1, Line 1; Eq. 7). The pipeline therefore remains solver-dependent.

The instance generator (Table 1) constructs b = Aξ + ε with ξ ~ randint[1,10], i.e., every instance embeds a known feasible solution that is nearly optimal. This makes the benchmark trivially easy and likely inflates the reported feasible rates and near-optimal gaps; there is no evidence the method works on harder or structured instances.

Evaluation is limited to two tiny synthetic dataset sizes (9x18 and 100x50 variables/constraints). No standard benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB, ML4CO competition instances) or real-world problems are used, so claims of generality are unsupported. 100x50 with 10% density and positive coefficients is far from the regime where MILP solving is actually hard.

There is no comparison against any ML-based baseline or prior RL work for MILP feasibility (e.g., Qi, Wang, and Shen 2021, which the authors themselves cite and whose instance generator they reuse). The only baselines are Gurobi and two architecture variants of their own method, so the contribution relative to the literature cannot be assessed.

The headline comparison with Gurobi is uninformative: Gurobi achieves 100/100 feasible and RP Gap 0/0.01 with first solutions in under 1 second, while the proposed method needs a 100-second budget to reach 1.33% gap on the larger set. The paper's own results show the method is strictly dominated by the solver it claims to replace.

The action space (increase/decrease by exactly 1 per variable per step) scales poorly; the paper provides no complexity or wall-clock analysis of how step requirements grow with instance size, and there is no generalization study (training and testing appear to be within the same distribution and size class).

Reproducibility is weak: no code release is mentioned, and key hyperparameters (number of GCN layers L, Transformer layers N, local region size Δ, step limits, learning rates, reward scaling constants) are not specified. Results appear to be single runs with no variance or statistical significance reported.

Novelty is modest: RL-guided local search over variable increments with feasibility-oriented rewards closely follows existing feasibility-pump-style and RL-for-MILP work; the Transformer-encoder component is an off-the-shelf architecture adaptation without empirical comparison to simpler attention-free designs at matched parameter counts beyond MLP/CNN.

Several experimental details are questionable or unexplained: the ablation table shows a configuration (PT without PE) finding 21/100 feasible with an 8.73% gap, but the interaction effects are not analyzed; FFST comparisons against Gurobi are admitted to be impossible due to missing sub-second timing yet are still tabulated as if comparable.

strengths: Clear and well-organized presentation: the problem motivation (feasibility of ML-based primal heuristics, handling non-binary integer variables) is well articulated, and the methodology (two-phase reward design, phase token, periodic embedding, hybrid MPNN+Transformer architecture) is described in sufficient detail to follow.

The two-phase reward design is a sensible and thoughtful contribution: separating learning objectives before/after the first feasible solution, with the LP-relaxation bound defining a target interval, is a reasonable formulation.

A reasonably thorough ablation study (Table 3) on PE, phase token, and separated actor/critic layers, with plausible explanations for observed failure modes (e.g., instability without PE, bias without phase information).
Honest limitations discussion: the authors acknowledge the restricted local search strategy, the difficulty of reaching global optima, and the restriction to all-integer variables.
The direction of end-to-end ML solvers that do not delegate sub-problems to commercial solvers is of genuine interest to the ML-for-optimization community.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is far too small to support the central claims. The largest testbed, D100*50 (100 variables, 50 constraints), is trivially easy: Gurobi solves all instances to (near-)optimality in under a second. Claims of 'solving MILP end-to-end based solely on ML' are not meaningfully demonstrated on instances where traditional solvers actually struggle. No standard benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB) or realistic problem classes are used.

The method does not actually eliminate reliance on traditional solvers, contradicting the framing: the search algorithm depends on an LP-relaxation solve for the initial solution and the lower bound obj_r (Algorithm 1, Line 1), and on rounding LP solutions. The abstract's claim of a solver 'based solely on ML' is overstated.

Baseline coverage is inadequate for the claimed novelty. The paper claims to be the first ML method to incrementally find better complete feasible solutions, yet compares only against Gurobi and internal MLP/CNN ablations. No comparison against prior RL-based work (e.g., Qi et al. 2021's smart feasibility pump, which uses the same instance generator) or ML-based primal heuristics (Gasse et al., Nair et al., Han et al.), even though these are discussed extensively.

Gurobi dominates on both metrics in Table 2 (RP Gap 0/0.01 vs. 1.33; FFST <1s vs. 0.06s), and since all methods find feasible solutions for 100/100 instances within a second, the practical advantage of the proposed approach remains unclear.

Severe scalability concerns are unaddressed: the action space changes each variable by ±1 per step, which appears poorly suited to larger variable ranges or unbounded variables (upper bounds are set to ∞ in the experiments); how the approach would scale to realistically sized MILPs is not analyzed.

Reproducibility gaps: no code release mentioned, key hyperparameters (layer counts, embedding dimensions, learning rates, step limits, local region size Δ) are unspecified, and no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported despite a small test set (100 instances per dataset).
Only a single synthetic instance distribution is used, with no out-of-distribution generalization experiments, despite the approach fundamentally relying on learning instance distributions.

Some methodological details are imprecise: the Actor-Critic description conflates value-based and policy-based components without clearly specifying the advantage estimator or loss; the reward design choices (e.g., the −10 exploration penalty, Case 2/3 asymmetries) are justified only narratively, not empirically.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: most ML-based primal heuristics focus on binary variables and delegate residual subproblems to traditional solvers. A full end-to-end RL approach that handles general integer variables and produces complete feasible solutions is a reasonable and under-explored direction.

The two-phase reward design (feasibility first, then optimality) is well-motivated and clearly explained, with a useful visual exposition (Appendix B) and explicit pseudo-code for both learning (Algorithm 1) and search (Algorithm 2), which supports reproducibility.

The hybrid MPNN + Transformer-encoder architecture is sensibly motivated (local structure via message passing, long-range variable interactions via attention, mitigating over-smoothing), and the ablation study (Table 3) examines each component individually.

The evaluation includes multiple metrics (feasibility rate, first feasible solution time, relative primal gap, #win), ablations over the toward-optimal bias parameter beta, neighborhood size, and architecture alternatives, showing internally consistent evidence that the learned agent outperforms the authors' own weaker baselines (LS, M.MLP, M.CNN) on their instance distributions.
Writing is generally clear, with good figures (e.g., Figure 4 on the RL interaction loop) and an honest related-work positioning relative to Qi et al. (2021).
weaknesses: Proposition 1 is essentially the standard LP-relaxation bound (obj_r <= obj_opt <= obj' < obj_b) and is trivially true; presenting it as a theoretical foundation for the method overstates its contribution. The claim of a method 'grounded in a theoretical foundation' is weak.

The central experimental evidence is limited to four small synthetic random MILP distributions (up to 300 variables x 100 constraints) generated by the authors. There are no standard benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB, ESC, real-world instances), so it is impossible to judge whether the approach generalizes beyond this narrow, easy problem family where Gurobi solves everything in under 1 second with near-zero gap.

The baseline comparison is weak. The only learning-based baselines (M.MLP, M.CNN) are the authors' own architecture ablations. Existing ML-based primal heuristics and end-to-end methods are excluded on the grounds of lacking integer-variable support, but relevant alternatives (e.g., Qi et al. 2021's smart feasibility pump, feasibility-pump-style baselines, or other RL/local-search hybrids) could have been adapted or compared; none are.

Practical significance is unclear: Gurobi achieves 100% FR and 0.00-0.03% gaps in under 1 second on all tested instances, strictly dominating the proposed solver, which additionally requires GPU infrastructure and training on the instance distribution. The paper does not identify any regime where the learned solver would be preferable (e.g., where solvers are slow, or amortized/inference-time benefits).

Although the method is framed as solver-free, it relies on the LP relaxation (x0, obj_r computed via a solver) for initialization and the reward/lower bound; this dependency on off-the-shelf LP machinery is not clearly acknowledged and slightly contradicts the 'without delegating to solvers' framing.
No variance reporting, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing for the results in Tables 1-3; differences such as Gap 0.34% vs 0.38% are interpreted without error bars.

Generalization is not evaluated: training and testing use the same random-instance distribution. Scalability of the Transformer attention to larger instances (O(n^2) over variable+constraint nodes) and behavior on instances with unbounded or negative-lower-bound variables (mentioned in passing but excluded by construction) remain open.

The scaling of the constraint-equality reward terms (Eqs. 7-10) and many hyperparameters (alpha, beta, penalty -10, delta sizes) are heuristic and hand-tuned; the paper offers limited justification or sensitivity analysis beyond the beta study.
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a system with many design choices.

strengths: Targets a genuinely under-explored problem: fully end-to-end learning for MILPs with general (non-binary) integer variables, where most ML-based primal heuristics must delegate to a solver to guarantee feasibility.

The RL formulation is clearly described: a well-defined observation/action/reward decomposition with a two-phase reward structure (first feasibility, then improvement toward the LP-relaxation lower bound), supported by pseudo-code (Algorithms 1-2) and illustrative examples (Figure 4, Appendix B).

The paper includes ablations (Table 3) on architectural components and a neighborhood-size study (Table 2), and discusses why a Transformer encoder is preferred over MPNNs (over-smoothing, distant variable interactions).
Writing and figures are generally clear; the setup details in Appendix E (data generation distributions, hardware, hyperparameters) exceed what many submissions provide.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution (Proposition 1) is trivial: the claim that any feasible solution's objective lies between the LP-relaxation optimum and the incumbent is a standard property of MILP relaxations, well known in branch-and-bound. Presenting this as a 'theoretical foundation' for the method overstates the contribution substantially.

Evaluation is confined to a single family of small, self-generated synthetic instances (up to 300 variables x 100 constraints, Table 4). No standard benchmarks (MIPLIB, set cover, maximum independent set, combinatorial auction, etc.) are used, so all claims of generality and near-optimality are unsupported beyond this narrow distribution.

Practical significance is unclear: Gurobi solves every test instance to (near-)optimality in under one second, while the proposed method uses a 100-second budget to achieve gaps of 0.3-0.7%. The paper does not identify any regime where the learned solver offers an advantage over an off-the-shelf solver, weakening the motivation for a full end-to-end approach.

Baselines are weak and comparisons are incomplete. The only comparisons are Gurobi, plain local search, and two custom MLP/CNN variants. No comparison is made to existing learned primal heuristics or RL feasibility approaches (e.g., Qi et al. 2021's smart feasibility pump, which the paper itself cites as the closest prior work; Nair et al. 2020's Neural Diving/branching). The claim of being the 'first full end-to-end RL-based solver' is asserted rather than substantiated experimentally.

Potential baseline miscalibration: M.CNN's feasible rate collapses to 0-4% on larger datasets while M.MLP retains 97-100%, which is suspicious and suggests the CNN baseline may be under-tuned rather than fundamentally incapable; no tuning effort or sensitivity analysis for baselines is reported.
No statistical rigor: results appear to be from single runs; no seeds, variance, or confidence intervals are reported, despite the stochastic nature of both RL training and instance generation.

The reward design is heavily engineered with many interacting hyperparameters (alpha, beta, the -10 stagnation penalty, bound rewards, delta scaling), but sensitivity analysis is limited to beta in {0.3, 0.6, 1} on small datasets; robustness of this reward shaping is unclear.

The action space (only +/-1 or +/-5 increments per variable) and the 'move back to the incumbent' mechanism make the method essentially a learned local search; its scalability to large-range integer variables, continuous variables, and realistic instance sizes is untested and not honestly addressed as a limitation.
No mention of code release, which, combined with the custom instance distribution, limits reproducibility.

Several overclaims are not supported by the evidence, e.g., that the work 'opens the door to a unified LP solver for multiple CO tasks' and that results 'demonstrate that the proposed method achieves (near-)optimal solutions' when the largest test cases are trivially solvable by Gurobi.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and under-explored problem: full end-to-end learning for MILPs with general (non-binary) integer variables, where most prior ML-based primal heuristics either delegate to solvers or handle only binary variables.

The RL formulation is carefully constructed: a two-phase reward design (feasibility first, then improvement toward the LP-relaxation bound) is sensible, well-motivated by Proposition 1, and clearly explained with visual aids (Appendix B).
The method requires no labeled data (unlike supervised predict-and-search approaches), which is a meaningful practical advantage.

The paper is generally well-written, with clear problem formulation, detailed pseudo-code (Algorithms 1-2), instance generation details, and a reasonable set of ablations (Transformer encoder, MPNN, periodic embedding, phase token) and hyperparameter studies (β, neighborhood size Δ).
The observation/action/reward design and the bipartite-graph-plus-Transformer architecture are described in enough detail to be reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: The scale of evaluation is very limited: all instances are small random synthetic MILPs (up to 300 variables and 100 constraints) that Gurobi solves in under 1 second to 0.01-0.03% gap. The claimed practical value of a learned solver on problems where an exact commercial solver is essentially instant is not established. No standard benchmarks (e.g., MIPLIB, MICO competition instances, or structured problem families like set cover, packing, scheduling) are used.

Baselines are weak. The only comparisons are local search and two ablated GNN variants (M.MLP, M.CNN) trained by the authors themselves. No comparison with existing learned primal heuristics (Nair et al. 2020, Gasse et al. 2019, Han et al. 2023, Cantürk et al. 2024) or the closest prior RL work (Qi et al. 2021) is provided; the stated justification (no integer-variable support / not standalone) is insufficient since adaptations are feasible and Qi et al. targets a closely related task.

The core 'theoretical foundation' (Proposition 1) is a standard, near-trivial consequence of the LP-relaxation bound (obj_r ≤ obj_opt ≤ obj') and does not constitute a substantial theoretical contribution; it supports but does not ground the search strategy in any deeper way.

Scalability of the action space is a concern: each step changes variables by at most ±1 (or ±Δ in Section 4.3), so reaching an optimum for variables with ranges [0, ∞) may require very long trajectories; behavior and convergence as problem size grows beyond the tested sizes is unclear. There is also no analysis of how the Transformer encoder scales to larger graphs.

The paper does not clarify a central question: is the policy trained per-instance-distribution and generalizing to unseen instances, or effectively retrained per instance? Training 'on-the-fly' per generated instance (Appendix E.1) suggests the latter, which would substantially limit practical deployment and should be made explicit.

The reward design introduces several sensitive hyperparameters (α, β, penalty constants like -10, Δ, T_grace) with limited sensitivity analysis; only β is ablated, and the report that β=1 behaves poorly on the smallest dataset suggests fragility.

Results in Table 1 are hard to interpret: '#win' is computed only among learned/LS methods excluding Gurobi, 'best gap' flags are inconsistent across β settings, and gaps on D_9x18 for baselines appear identical across β, raising questions about variance/seeds; no error bars or multiple seeds for evaluation are reported.

The abstract/intro framing ('opens the door to a unified LP solver for multiple CO tasks') overreaches relative to what is demonstrated — a single synthetic instance family with a specific coefficient distribution.
No code release is stated, and no limitations section is included, which weakens reproducibility and transparency for a method with this many design choices.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clearly motivated gap: existing end-to-end learning-based primal heuristics cannot independently generate feasible solutions and largely ignore non-binary integer variables, while RL-SPH learns feasibility directly and handles general integers.

The method is well-motivated and clearly presented: a two-phase reward design (feasibility first, then incumbent improvement), phase-separated actor/critic heads, and a variable-selection search strategy are described in detail with helpful figures, pseudocode (Algorithms 1-3), and implementation details (Appendix E).

Reasonably thorough experiments: comparisons against four classical start primal heuristics (Diving, FP, Rounding, RENS), a combination experiment with SCIP against PAS+S, an ablation over GNN components (Table 3), and a hyperparameter study on the toward-optimal bias (Table 7).

The finding that RL-SPH works even from random initialization (comparable to LP initialization) is a practically interesting result, suggesting the learned policy genuinely repairs infeasible solutions.
Honest limitations discussion, e.g., acknowledging that variable fixing may introduce sub-optimality and that RL-SPH underperforms on set covering (SC) in Table 1.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not actually established. Proposition 1 assumes R_const > 0 and R_bound = 0 for ALL t < T, which essentially assumes the monotone feasibility improvement the method is supposed to achieve. Moreover, the proof is mathematically flawed: a monotonically increasing sequence upper-bounded by 0 converges to some limit <= 0, not necessarily 0 as claimed, so 'lim -> 0' does not follow. Claims of 'theoretically guaranteeing feasibility' in the abstract and conclusion are therefore overstated.

Baseline comparability is questionable in Table 1: SCIP heuristics are run on CPU with presolving and branching disabled, while RL-SPH uses a GPU (A100) and stops only 'when all baseline methods complete.' Time-based metrics (PI) and the 44x/2.3x headline claims are hard to interpret without equivalent hardware accounting.

Aggregate claims mask per-dataset weaknesses: on SC, Diving and RENS achieve PG = 0.00 vs. RL-SPH's 9.67-12.78, yet the abstract reports an average '44x lower primal gap.' The averaged statistic is driven by a few datasets (IS, MVC, NBI) and does not reflect uniform superiority.

Limited external validity: all benchmarks are synthetic and moderate-sized (2,000-4,000 variables); only one learning-based baseline (PAS) is compared; there are no generalization experiments (e.g., cross-distribution transfer) despite the agent being trained per problem class with only 1,000 training instances.

Scalability of the action design is unexamined: unit-increment (+/-1) actions with only ~2*log2(n) changeable variables per step may be slow for integer variables with wide domains, and only one synthetic non-binary dataset (NBI) is used to support the central claim about integer variables.
No release of the authors' own code is mentioned, limiting reproducibility despite detailed implementation notes.

Minor presentation issues: Section 4 states 'two experiments' but then lists three; the PI metric definition (averaged only over instances with at least one feasible solution, with PG=1 substitution) is nonstandard and complicates cross-paper comparison.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and under-explored problem: learning-based primal heuristics that can independently produce feasible solutions (rather than requiring an ILP solver to repair partial predictions) and that extend beyond binary variables.

The RL formulation is clearly described: a two-phase reward design (feasibility first, then incumbent improvement), phase-separated actor/critic layers, and a variable-selection strategy are all specified in enough detail (Algorithms 1–3, Appendices B–D) that the method is understandable and largely re-implementable.

The evaluation includes useful components beyond a single headline table: an ablation study on the GNN components (Table 3), a study of the toward-optimal bias (Table 7), training-time reporting (Table 6), and both LP and random initializations (Table 1), which is more thorough than many ML4CO papers.

The honest discussion of limitations (e.g., potential sub-optimality from fixing variables in Section 4.3) is appropriate, and RL-SPH(Random) performing comparably to RL-SPH(LP) is an interesting empirical finding.
weaknesses: The headline claim of a '44× lower primal gap' is misleading. It is computed only against baselines with 100% feasibility rate, and Table 1 actually shows RL-SPH losing to Diving and RENS on SC (PG 0.00 vs 9.67–12.78). Averaging across heterogeneous benchmarks to produce a single '44×' figure obscures rather than supports the claim of superiority.

The 'theoretical guarantee' of feasibility — presented as a central contribution and repeated in the conclusion — is not sound. Proposition 1 assumes exactly the conclusion-driving conditions (Rt,const > 0 and Rt,bound = 0 for all t < T), which the agent is never shown to satisfy; moreover, the proof's claim that a monotonically increasing sequence upper-bounded by 0 has limit 0 is mathematically incorrect (it converges to some limit ≤ 0). The proposition is essentially vacuous as stated.

The paper's motivating gap — handling non-binary integer variables — is barely evaluated. Four of five benchmarks (IS, CA, SC, MVC) are purely binary, and the non-binary (NBI) experiment appears only in Table 2 against a single baseline (SCIP), with no E2EPH comparison (PAS is marked N/A) and no experiment in Table 1. The central claim rests on one synthetic dataset generated by the authors.

There is no generalization evaluation. A distinct model is trained per benchmark on 1,000 in-distribution instances (~30–80 minutes each), while the SCIP baselines are generic. For a learned heuristic, performance on unseen distributions or instance sizes is the critical question and is entirely unaddressed.

The formulation restricts to pure ILP (all variables integer, Eq. 1c), i.e., MILPs with continuous variables — the most common practical case — are out of scope, yet the abstract and introduction claim contributions for 'ILP' broadly. Similarly, the fixed action magnitude of ±1 raises scalability concerns for integer variables with wide ranges that are not discussed.

The claim of being 'the first E2EPH method that explicitly learns feasibility' is overstated without engaging Qi et al. (2021)'s Smart Feasibility Pump, an RL-based feasibility method that the authors cite but only use for instance generation, without comparison or discussion.

The solver-integration experiment (Table 2) covers only two of five benchmarks, and no explanation is given for the omission of CA, SC, and MVC — precisely where Table 1 suggests the method may be weakest. The +S ensemble/fixing procedure is also under-specified.

Experimental fairness concerns: SCIP baselines run heuristics in isolation with presolving/branching disabled, while RL-SPH uses an A100 GPU and per-dataset training; the text also says 'two experiments' while describing three, and the abstract claims 100% FR on 'five benchmarks' while Table 1 reports four.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: existing end-to-end learning-based primal heuristics rely on an ILP solver to repair infeasible predictions and largely handle only binary variables. Proposing a start primal heuristic that independently generates feasible solutions, including for non-binary integers, is a meaningful and useful contribution to the ML-for-CO literature.

The methodology is described in unusual depth: the RL formulation (observation, action, two-phase reward design), the phase-separated actor-critic architecture, the variable-selection strategy (Algorithm 3), the learning procedure (Algorithm 2), and the search strategy (Algorithm 1) are all fully specified, which supports reproducibility. Training times, hyperparameters, hardware, randomization settings, and code sources are provided.

The experimental protocol is reasonably thorough: five benchmarks (including a non-binary-integer dataset), three metrics (FR, PG, PI), comparison against SCIP's built-in start heuristics, an integration experiment against SCIP and PAS+SCIP, an architecture ablation (Table 3), and a sensitivity study on the toward-optimal bias (Table 7). The result that RL-SPH(Random) matches RL-SPH(LP) is an interesting and practically relevant finding.

The writing is clear, with helpful figures (e.g., Figure 3 illustrating the RL interaction) and an honest limitations discussion (e.g., acknowledging potential sub-optimality from variable fixing in Section 4.3).
weaknesses: The novelty claim that RL-SPH is 'the first E2EPH method that explicitly learns feasibility for ILP' is overstated and under-defended. Qi et al. (2021) (Smart Feasibility Pump), which the authors themselves cite for instance generation, applies RL to feasibility pumping for ILP, yet it is neither discussed as prior art nor included as a baseline. The comparison to learning-based baselines is limited to PAS alone; this weakens the empirical support for the central novelty claim.

Proposition 1 is weak and arguably circular. It assumes R_{t,const} > 0 and R_{t,bound} = 0 for all t < T (i.e., strictly monotone feasibility improvement) and then concludes feasibility at T. The proof is a trivial monotone-convergence argument; the nontrivial question—whether the trained agent actually achieves these conditions—is not established. Presenting this as 'theoretically guaranteeing feasibility' in the conclusion overstates what the theory supports.

Training is per-dataset (a separate agent per benchmark), and there is no evaluation of generalization across problem families or instance sizes, which is a significant practical limitation for a learned primal heuristic. All instances are synthetic; standard hard instance libraries (e.g., MIPLIB) or real-world MILPs are absent, limiting evidence of practical reach.

Several fairness and consistency concerns in the evaluation: (i) baselines run on CPU via SCIP while RL-SPH uses an A100 GPU, complicating time-based metrics (PI); (ii) PG/PI are averaged only over instances where at least one method found a feasible solution, introducing selection bias that interacts unequally with FR; (iii) the abstract claims 'four CO benchmarks' while Section 4.1.1 lists five, and Section 4 says 'two experiments' then enumerates three; (iv) in Table 2 on NBI, the PG of RL-SPH+S (0.23) is essentially identical to SCIP (0.24), yet the text claims RL-SPH+S 'outperformed both SCIP and PAS+S in terms of PG and PI on both benchmarks'—the PG advantage is marginal and within noise given the reported deviations.

The reward design is highly hand-tuned (penalty -100, phase-specific case tables with α=2, bound/constraint reward scaling by 1/√ñ), yet sensitivity analysis is provided only for α. The complexity and brittleness of this reward engineering are not examined. Additionally, the extremely low FR of Diving/RENS on SC (1-3%) in Table 1 raises questions about baseline configuration that the paper does not probe.

Scalability of the Transformer-based agent is not analyzed: attention over bipartite graphs with up to 4,000 variables and ~12,000 constraints has non-trivial memory and inference cost per step, and inference-time overhead relative to classical heuristics is not quantified.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the paper identifies a genuine gap—existing E2E2PH methods delegate feasibility to external solvers and largely target binary variables—and positions RL-SPH as a standalone start primal heuristic that produces ILP-feasible solutions itself, including for non-binary integers.

The two-phase reward design (phase1 feasibility-first, phase2 objective improvement) is coherent, well-justified (Appendix F), and supported by Proposition 1 plus an empirical adherence-rate analysis (Table 3, 88–99% adherence), which connects theory to practice rather than leaving the reward design purely heuristic.

Comprehensive and unusually thorough evaluation: 5 NP-hard benchmarks including a non-binary integer dataset, comparison against 15 diving + 6 rounding SCIP heuristics and 3 SOTA E2E2PH methods, ablations on both the search strategy and ILP-GT architecture, cross-problem generalization, distribution/size/density shift tests, MIPLIB evaluation, and integration with SCIP and Gurobi (Tables 16–17).

Practical efficiency: no supervised labels required, ~30 min average training time, consistent hyperparameters across all datasets (vs. benchmark-specific tuning for baselines), with training-time comparisons reported against PAS, DDIM, and DiffILO (Table 10).

Honest and detailed limitations discussion (Appendices I.1–I.8), including scalability bottlenecks at extreme sizes, weaknesses on specific MIPLIB instances (e.g., scpk4), and the action-magnitude restriction (Δx=1).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is modest: Proposition 1 is a relatively straightforward argument that holds only under the assumption that a well-trained agent maximizes rewards; it is a conditional alignment argument, not a feasibility guarantee, and the headline framing of 'theoretical reward-feasibility alignment' slightly overstates its strength.

Evaluation is dominated by synthetic benchmarks; the MIPLIB evaluation is limited to 17 instances, and solution quality on some of them is substantially worse than baselines (e.g., scpk4 incumbent 13,672 vs. BKS 318), indicating limited objective-value quality on harder, larger, or structurally different instances.

Single-problem models achieve 0% feasibility rate on the other problem in cross-problem tests (Table 4); generalization is achieved only via joint training, so zero-shot generalization across problem classes remains unresolved.

The architecture (Graph Transformer + actor-critic) and RL machinery are largely standard; novelty rests mainly on the reward design and feasibility-aware variable selection, and the core comparison (Table 1) shows most baselines also reach 100% FR given a 1,000-second limit, so the FR advantage is partly attributable to the generous time budget and initialization.

E2E2PH baselines are trained with their own configurations on the authors' datasets, which differ in size from those used in the original papers (Table 11); while the authors argue this reasonably, some uncertainty remains about whether DiffILO/PAS were given the most favorable conditions.
No explicit code-release statement for RL-SPH itself is visible in the manuscript, which limits reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameter reporting.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and clearly motivated gap: learned start primal heuristics that generate feasible solutions *independently* of an external ILP solver, including problems with non-binary integer variables, which existing E2EPH methods largely avoid by delegating feasibility to solvers.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: five benchmarks, 15 diving and 6 rounding heuristic variants from SCIP as SPH baselines, three representative E2EPH baselines (PAS, DDIM, DiffILO), ablations of both the search strategy and the architecture, cross-problem generalization, distribution/size/density shifts, MIPLIB evaluation, and solver-integration experiments (SCIP and Gurobi).

The claimed 100% feasibility rate is consistently supported across the reported tables, and the phase-separated reward design (feasibility first, then objective improvement) is empirically validated via adherence rates (Table 3) and qualitative trajectory analyses (Figure 10).

Reproducibility is well treated: hyperparameters are held fixed across datasets (a notable advantage over benchmark-tuned baselines), training times, model sizes, instance-generation parameters, and evaluation environments are all documented, and baselines are run with released official code.

Training efficiency is a practical advantage: no near-optimal solution labels are needed, and training takes under ~90 minutes per benchmark, compared to hours for supervised or diffusion-based baselines (Table 10).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is essentially circular. Proposition 1 assumes R_t,const > 0 at every step (i.e., that the agent makes feasibility-improving moves) and then concludes feasibility is eventually reached. This does not establish that the learned policy can or will produce such improving moves; it is a restatement of a greedy descent argument on a discrete measure, so the 'theoretical reward–feasibility alignment' claim is oversold.

Comparison setups contain potentially favorable choices that weaken the headline numbers. The reported PG/PI improvements are 'averaged over Dataset-Baseline pairs with 100% FR,' which filters out the hardest instances where baselines fail, potentially inflating the 28.6× gap; the 100-second budget and termination conditions differ across methods; and the E2EPH baselines were evaluated on benchmarks whose sizes differ substantially from their original papers (Table 11), which the authors acknowledge may have degraded DiffILO.

The method is mostly trained per-dataset for the main results; the joint IS+MVC model is the only cross-problem result in the main text, and MIPLIB results reveal significant weaknesses on out-of-distribution instances (e.g., scpk4 incumbent 13,672 vs. BKS 318; bppc8-02 with set-partitioning constraints), indicating the generalization claims should be interpreted cautiously.

Novelty is moderate: the core loop—RL agent iteratively perturbing a subset of variables guided by constraint-violation signals—closely mirrors NeuRewriter-style rewriting and learning-based LNS, extended to the infeasible-start setting with a phase-separated reward. The Graph Transformer (ILP-GT) is a fairly standard architecture with domain-specific input features (boundary flags, periodic embeddings, reward-context tokens), as the ablation Table 6 partially confirms (component contributions vary).

Scalability and action-space restrictions limit practical reach: movement magnitude is fixed at ±1 (larger magnitudes are only explored in a small 100-variable side experiment, Table 22), the feasibility-aware variable selection is O(mn) and becomes a bottleneck when m ≈ n (Appendix I.4–I.5), and these limitations are deferred to future work rather than resolved.

Several design choices are justified primarily by empirical tuning (e.g., the heavy −100 stagnation penalty, α = 2 toward-optimal bias, √n̄ scaling of the bound penalty), and the sensitivity analyses show performance degrades non-trivially with these choices (e.g., α = 5 on SC), suggesting some brittleness.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: learning-based start primal heuristics that can independently generate feasible ILP solutions without delegating feasibility to an external solver, and it handles non-binary integer variables, which prior E2EPH methods do not support.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive: five benchmarks, four SPH baselines (15 diving and 6 rounding variants grouped into DHF/RHF), three recent E2EPH baselines (PAS, DDIM, DiffILO), cross-problem generalization, distribution/size/density shift tests, 17 MIPLIB instances, integration with SCIP and Gurobi, ablations of the search strategy and ILP-GT components, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses.

The two-phase reward design (phase1: reach feasibility; phase2: improve the incumbent) is well motivated, and the paper provides both a theoretical argument (Proposition 1) and an empirical adherence-rate analysis (Table 3, 88-99%) connecting the reward to feasibility-seeking behavior.

Training efficiency is a real practical advantage: ~30 minutes per dataset with no supervised labels, and a single hyperparameter configuration across all benchmarks, contrasting with benchmark-specific tuning needed for E2EPH baselines.
The limitations discussion is reasonably honest, e.g., acknowledging failure on scpk4, difficulty with Set Partitioning constraints absent from training, and the O(mn) variable-selection bottleneck.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weaker than advertised. Proposition 1 essentially states that monotone improvement in constraint slack eventually reaches feasibility; this is a near-trivial consequence of discreteness and assumes exactly the behavior (Rt,const > 0 and Rt,bound = 0 at every step) that a trained agent is not guaranteed to exhibit. Calling this the first 'theoretical reward-feasibility alignment' for E2EPH overstates its depth; it does not establish convergence of the RL policy itself.

The action space (unit-magnitude ±1 moves on n-tilde ≈ 2⌈log2 n⌉ changeable variables) is restrictive for large-range integer variables, and the repair-based search raises a fundamental scalability concern. This materializes in the MIPLIB experiments, where solution quality is mixed (e.g., incumbent 13,672 vs. BKS 318 on scpk4; worse incumbents than RHF on several instances such as toll-like, queens-30, rail507), so the '100% FR with high quality' narrative does not fully carry over to realistic instances.

Benchmark coverage is largely synthetic. Only one non-binary dataset (a generated multidimensional knapsack) supports the headline integer-variable claim, and real-world evidence rests on 17 hand-picked MIPLIB instances.

Some comparisons raise fairness concerns. SCIP baselines run with presolving and branching disabled to isolate heuristics, while RL-SPH runs on a GPU; and the E2EPH baselines are trained with default configurations on datasets whose characteristics differ substantially from their original studies (e.g., CA with ~2.7x more variables), which the authors themselves argue necessitates retuning for DiffILO. Attributing DiffILO's 0% FR partly to dataset mismatch is somewhat circular.

Methodological novelty is incremental: the core is an actor-critic agent performing learned local search with a hand-crafted feasibility reward and a heuristic (non-learned) variable-selection strategy; ILP-GT is a fairly standard graph transformer with periodic embeddings. Many reward design choices (α=2, the -100 stagnation penalty, phase priorities, 1/√n scaling) are justified empirically rather than derived, and several interact in ways the theory does not cover.

Reproducibility could be stronger: the paper details baselines' code and hyperparameters thoroughly, but there is no explicit statement that RL-SPH's own code, training data, or trained checkpoints will be released.
